summary: Lifeline is a website we created to help astronauts track, analyze, interpret, and understand their crucial health metrics, paired with a custom-coded Gemini model. Astronauts face lots of health risks and challenges while on their mission, and might not have the necessary information/knowledge or time to manage it by themselves. Our goal is to support astronaut health on missions, and we hope to combine health and technology to make astronauts’ lives a little bit safer and easier! Additionally, Lifeline is important because travel time when communicating with the ground team on Earth can become excessive depending on where the mission takes the astronauts, which is incredibly risky and inefficient. Lifeline lets astronauts discover and handle their problems independently, allowing for them to focus on their mission. Lifeline also compares the data across the crew members to get a comprehensive idea of any common issues that may be because of the environment. This website allows them to track all of their metrics over time, analyze and understand what each means, and also give information and guidance in case of emergencies, thus improving the overall quality of our space endeavors.
details:
We hope Lifeline can help astronauts independently monitor, analyze, interpret, and understand their own health metrics efficiently and quickly, without needing to refer back to the ground. As a general goal, we also strive to better support astronauts, making their missions smoother and safer. Lifeline not only helps manage health metrics, but also teaches the user how to take measurements, how to interpret the metrics (as healthy, moderate, or critical), gives information in a clear way, and personalized recommendations to stay healthy during the mission. It’s clear, intuitive, concise, and fun to use, with mini-games, color-coding, and lots of interactive diagrams. See project demonstration slide 3-4 for a concise summary of all benefits. When building Lifeline, we researched and read lots of articles, websites, studies, and field reports in order to better understand the challenges and risks that astronauts face, which we then incorporated through choosing relevant and helpful metrics along with developing a custom Gemini model to give astronauts a concise overview. 

The Lifeline tab gives an overall trend of everything, using Earth, Jupiter, and Mars to sort people into different categories of health. It also displays a color-coded data grid, to show which metrics are dragging down their lifeline or are normal. We included what-if sliders to simulate how certain changes in their metrics could affect their lifeline score, allowing them to plan for the best benefits in the future.

Routine tab has a little minigame, gives you achievements, streaks, points, and since there’s no reward for being healthy there’s no pressure to lie for more points. This prioritizes honesty which then leads to more accurate data for each person, overall assisting the astronauts better. Also, we added in a tiny animation once they complete all their tasks, so they can have the satisfaction of completing things, checking things off list, leading to more motivation and a more fun experience. This encourages accountability, honesty, and makes them happy!!

The emergency part includes a timer so that in the event that an astronaut inputs a critical value, which may be due to a typo, simple mistake, incorrect administration of their test, or another source of error that doesn’t reflect their true metric. This timer gives them a little grace period to redo the assessment before triggering the emergency warning. However, for certain values, the timer is skipped since it’s too dangerous or because correcting it wouldn’t have a huge impact. This allows them to avoid false alarms or invalidating their data while also not disregarding their needs if the emergency was indeed happening. 

We also included filters for different environments, crew members, and a dynamic background that we put a lot of effort into (with a logo that fits the theme of a Lifeline and space). Additionally, we created a crew orbit tab which serves as a status checker that you can click on to see each person’s main metrics, dashboard, and lifeline, while also seeing everyone’s status as a whole. Astronauts logging their vitals are done through different forms of input, including smiley faces to gauge overall mood and numbers, as well as a clicker test for reaction time. 

We utilized Google Cloud Console for the custom Gemini model, FastAPI, Pydantic, Google Scholar and Google for research, NASA websites, Google Docs for planning and organization, Github for sharing code, Canvas for background aesthetics, Google Fonts, svg for vector graphics (like planets, charts, etc), Kapwing for subtitles, Vercel for hosting our website, Claude for editing and debugging our code/notes and to setup the backbone, basic framework, and then we added our own personalizations, features, backend code, diagrams, model, and ideas! We coded the frontend with HTML, CSS, and Javascript, and used Python for the backend. 

There are multiple environments to run the website in, and also different crew members, each with their unique metrics/profile/data. Additionally, for this hackathon, we created multiple scenarios, so you can see what the website would look like in normal situations, situations where some of the crew have vision changes, many of the crew have CO2 related headaches, and more. 

DETAILED BREAKDOWN OF EACH TAB

Dashboard Tab: Displays a general assessment of each person’s “health”/lifeline, general statistics about the crew and environment, and an overview of the recent metrics readings. 

Learn Tab: we compiled all of our notes and discoveries from various NASA websites, field reports, research papers, and other resources we looked at to tell astronauts what each metric is, how to measure it, why it matters, what could go wrong, what to do to avoid it turning into a critical condition, and the limitations of the metric. 

Health Assessment Tab: generates the AI overview, a personalized summary for metrics to monitor, and even a score for context (how “weird” today’s readings are from the crew member’s typical metrics).  

Log Vitals: Can input the metrics and symptoms, click on the i button for information about the metric. Once you press save and assess, our backend code runs to do 2 things. First, we’ve “hardcoded” (manually coded with a bunch of conditionals) our website to determine when a metric has passed the critical thresholds. If it is outside the thresholds, we first confirm that the readings are correct and not a typo, then skip the AI overview and go directly into Emergency mode. 

Emergency mode/tab: we show what to do immediately for the given emergency, information/guides, a button to send a comprehensive report to the flight surgeon (since we aren’t on an actual mission, you just have a button to copy it), a button to report the crew, and, if necessary, a reminder and timer to recheck their metrics/vitals. We carefully coded the backend to skip the AI overview, saving time and prioritizing the recovery/stabilization of the person. If none of the metrics have passed the critical threshold, we included a custom-coded Gemini model that will look at all of the reported metrics together. For instance, if a few metrics are slightly away from optimal levels, they will look at them comprehensively to figure out what might be happening, giving a concise explanation, personalized recommendations, and metrics to keep an eye on. 

Crew Orbit:

Body Map: We made an interactive body map so that astronauts can engage with the different parts included in it and see how they’re doing. It’s also color-coded in order to draw attention to certain parts that are at risk and to overall help with the understanding of its status at a glance. For example, if a crew member notices their vision’s been feeling off, they can click on the eyes in the body  map to see what their latest measurements are. Doing this also redirects the astronauts to info pages and recommendations so that they are fully knowledgeable of their condition and what they can do about it. 

Lifeline: This tab shows how a certain member’s health trends over time, with that time depending on a range they can choose of either 14 or 30 days. There are filters that can be applied to get smaller, more specific line graphs for each metric that the astronauts can compare. Additionally, we included sliders to show astronauts what their lifelines would look like under certain “What if” conditions that they can control, just to give them a more complete picture of how their health can change.

Routine: Everyone gets a checklist that has all of the tasks they should be doing everyday to keep them healthy and monitored. It’s a mini game in the sense that there are points, streak rewards, achievements and a celebration animation every time they complete the list. This is to encourage the astronauts to do these tasks by making it slightly more fun and less of a to-do list. Also, there are no rewards for feeling “better,” which gives each member the freedom to be truthful about everything they’re feeling instead of trying to lie about their status just to get points.
